summary:
Outpost Red is a browser-based Mars survival game that lets students run a four-person outpost. Our aim is to make real engineering trade-offs tangible and fun for young learners.
We built it because space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies how missions work, or presents them at a level too complex for a young learner's attention. Few tools sit in between.
Outpost Red solves this challenge with a simple loop. Each sol, students spend six work points across power, life support, radiation shielding and food, while a forecast warns of dust storms, solar flares, scrubber failures and crop blight. Low power drains air and food, so one neglected system drags down the others. Credits buy upgrades, but only three of four are affordable, forcing hard choices. After each event, a NASA fact explains the real science, drawn from Curiosity radiation data, the Opportunity dust storm and ISS Veggie and air systems.
It matters because students learn firsthand that missions succeed through balance, not perfect answers. It runs in any browser on phones and laptops, with no installation.
details:
What it does: Outpost Red is a browser-based Mars survival game. Students act as chief engineer of a four-person outpost and, over 15 sols, spend six work points a day to keep power, life support, radiation shielding and food running. A daily forecast warns of dust storms, solar flares, scrubber failures and crop blight. Low power drains air and food, so one weak system drags down the others. Credits buy upgrades, but only three of four are affordable, which forces real trade-offs.

Benefits and impact: Students experience the decisions that decide whether a mission fails or succeeds, instead of just reading about them. Each event ends with a NASA fact, so play turns into learning.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with canvas animation and inline SVG graphics. It runs on phones and laptops with no install. Code was written with help from Claude, an AI assistant.

Creativity: An animated rocket launch, a live Mars base scene, and a crew of four with specialist roles.

Factors considered: Simple rules for junior learners, scientific accuracy based on Curiosity radiation data, the Opportunity dust storm and the ISS Veggie and air systems, reduced-motion support, and large touch buttons.
